On physical examination, he is afebrile, with a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation is 94% on room air.
Lung auscultation reveals decreased breath sounds in the right upper lobe.
A chest X-ray shows a 2 cm nodule in the right upper lobe.
A computed tomography (CT) scan of the chest confirms the presence of the nodule with spiculated margins.
The patient undergoes a CT-guided biopsy of the nodule, and cytology is suspicious for malignancy.
The patient is referred to an oncologist for further evaluation.
The oncologist is considering a serum tumor marker test to aid in the diagnosis.

lines: Fatigue, decreased appetite, abdominal discomfort, and yellowing of eyes

Family history is notable for his father's death from myocardial infarction at age 63 and his mother's death from breast cancer at age 70.
The patient works as a construction foreman and says his job is stressful, often leading him to have "a few beers" after work.
On further questioning, he admits to drinking 8–10 beers daily for more than 25 years, with occasional whiskey on weekends.
He smokes one pack of cigarettes per day and has done so for 30 years.
His diet consists mainly of fast food and processed snacks, and he rarely exercises.
Review of systems is notable for mild difficulty sleeping, decreased libido, and occasional easy bruising.
There is no history of hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia.
He denies chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath.
Vital signs: temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure 138/84 mm Hg, pulse 88/min, respirations 18/min.
On physical examination, the patient appears tired but alert.
There is mild scleral icterus, palmar erythema, and multiple spider angiomata over the upper chest and shoulders.
The abdomen is soft but mildly distended, with a liver edge palpable 3 cm below the right costal margin; the liver is firm and mildly tender.
Hepatitis B and C serologies are negative.
Abdominal ultrasound shows an enlarged liver with heterogeneous echotexture, no focal masses, and patent hepatic vessels.
A liver biopsy is performed to evaluate the degree of inflammation and fibrosis.
Histopathology demonstrates swollen hepatocytes with ballooning degeneration, infiltration by neutrophils, and irregular, rope-like eosinophilic inclusions in the cytoplasm.
- Non-small cell lung cancer, right upper lobe (diagnosed 2021-03-15)
- Peripheral artery disease (aortoiliac occlusive disease/Leriche syndrome)

- Father with alcohol use disorder and cirrhosis
- Mother with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Widespread hepatocyte injury with activation of apoptosis.
Further analysis demonstrates increased mitochondrial membrane permeability and release of a specific mitochondrial protein into the cytosol that triggers cell death.
